short: The century in which a country of a million and a half people ran the Baltic.
full:
Sweden's great power period - stormaktstiden - is conventionally dated from the accession of Gustavus Adolphus in 1611 to the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. At its height the empire held Finland, Estonia, Livonia, Ingria, Western Pomerania, Bremen-Verden and Wismar, and the Baltic was close to a Swedish lake. It rested on a small population, perhaps a million and a half in Sweden proper, and was paid for by tolls levied on the trade passing through its captured ports, by copper and iron exports, and by French subsidies.

The machinery was unusually efficient for the age. Parish conscription, the allotment system that settled soldiers on farms, and a working central bureaucracy let Sweden field armies out of all proportion to its wealth. The weakness was the same fact. The empire depended on continuous military success and on foreign money, so when Denmark, Saxony-Poland and Russia attacked together in 1700, and the field army was destroyed at Poltava in 1709, there were no reserves of population or credit to replace it.
